passage:
So, Nilesh, you asked me once what my worst online moment was. It's this. I'm Gurleen, and last spring I shared a post saying a girl called Meher from another college had cheated in an exam. It had a screenshot, and it was angry, and it felt like standing up for fairness. I didn't check it.

Two days later a friend sent me the college's statement: it was false. By then Meher was getting messages I wouldn't wish on anyone. My stomach dropped. My first thought was to say "well, I only shared it."

I didn't. I deleted it that night, posted a plain correction saying the claim was false and I was sorry I spread it, and messaged Meher directly to apologise. She read it and didn't reply. I understand.

qa.q: What did the post Gurleen shared claim about Meher?
qa.a: The post said Meher, a girl from another college, had cheated in an exam.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when the college's statement arrived, and what did Gurleen first want to say?
qa.a: Gurleen felt sick and ashamed, and first wanted to say "well, I only shared it", which was a way of protecting pride.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that was right, and what else could help?
qa.a: Gurleen deleted the post, posted a plain correction and apologised to Meher directly; checking claims before sharing would help next time. 🤍

qa.q: How might Meher see Gurleen's apology?
qa.a: Meher read it and did not reply, which could mean she is still hurt by what happened, and Gurleen accepts that her silence is fair.

grounding: Gurleen realises a shared false claim hurt a person, feels ashamed, deletes it, posts a plain correction and apologises to her instead of defending it out of pride.

The panchayat group in Sonpur had two hundred members, and Usha had forwarded the message to all of them: the anganwadi worker, Shabnam didi, was selling the children's ration packets in the next village.

Two days later Rafiq, who drove the school van, stopped her outside the dairy. "Usha, the ration van was late all month. The block office confirmed it. Shabnam didi has been paying for biscuits herself."

Usha's face went hot. Her first thought was, everyone else forwarded it too. She almost said it aloud. Instead she took out her phone right there, deleted the forward and typed a correction in the same group: "What I shared about Shabnam didi was false. I am sorry."

That evening she walked to the anganwadi with her little brother. Shabnam didi listened, arms folded, and then nodded once.

qa.q: What did the forwarded message accuse Shabnam didi of?
qa.a: It said she was selling the children's ration packets in the next village.

qa.q: What was Usha tempted to say when she heard the truth, and what does that show?
qa.a: Usha wanted to say everyone else forwarded it too, which shows embarrassment and a wish to protect her pride from shame.

qa.q: What did Usha do well after learning the truth?
qa.a: Usha deleted the forward, posted a plain correction in the same group, and went to apologise in person the same evening.

qa.q: How might Shabnam didi have felt during the two days before the correction?
qa.a: Shabnam didi likely felt wronged and humiliated, having been accused of stealing while she was actually spending her own money on the children.

grounding: The story shows a young woman who spread a false claim feeling ashamed, resisting the pull to defend it, correcting it and apologising.
